words.lemma: míl 'animal, beast' (nom. sg.; not míl 'louse', not míl 'soldier')

cognate: OIr bó ~ Gk βοῦς (*gʷōu-); OIr míl ~ Gk μῆλον (*meh₁lo- 'small livestock / beast'; cf. W mil 'animal', Arm. mal 'sheep')
drift_or_renewal: Irish míl has widened to 'beast, animal' in general; Greek μῆλα keeps the narrow sense 'sheep and goats'. The Irish context (the animals are milked) still shows the pastoral sense.
shared_syntax: two coordinated nouns for kinds of livestock: Ir. cech bó ocus cech míl (subject of a relative verb) ~ Gk μῆλα καὶ (ἕλικας) βοῦς (object), with the order reversed in Greek
context: Both are pastoral: in Longes mac nUislenn the singing of the sons of Uisliu makes every cow and every beast that hears it give two thirds more milk; in Homer and Hesiod the pair names the herd as a whole (watched by herdsmen on the Shield, slaughtered at the pyre, tamed on the right day).
phrase: *gʷōus + *meh₁lo- 'cattle and small stock' as a livestock merism
note: In the Celtic layer the Irish collocation occurs only in this one passage (three witnesses of the same text), and I found nothing similar in Welsh (W mil there is 'thousand'). Pairing 'cattle and (other) beasts' could arise independently. The claim rests on both members being cognate and on the Greek formula (μῆλα καὶ βοῦς, βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα) being well established.

All 300 bundles read. Most are livestock-tribute lists from Lebor na Cert set against one MBh line, Cato, or legal/annalistic prose; these hold no shared wording. One low-confidence claim. Considered and rejected: duille ocus bláth ~ floribus et foliis / φύλλοισι τεθηλώς (BS-b50c6, BS-ce780): a generic and hagiographic merism with disputed cognacy. Also rejected: toilg menman ... i cridi ~ hṛdā manasā (BS-83dca), not coordinated, and menmae is not < *ménos; snáifid sruth ~ sneha sravān prasravati (BS-dd811), different verbs.
